## Revision aids
The first of Foolscap's revision aids: they find the words you lean on and mark them for you to judge. They never change or suggest a word.
- **View › Revision Highlights** tints, in the text, a kind of thing to look at: **Echoes** (a word used again close by), **Overused Words**, **Repeated Phrases**, your **Watch List**, **Long Sentences**, and in English, **Adverbs**, **Passive Voice**, **Filter Verbs** and **Dialogue Tags**. - **A highlight bar** under the editor's header shows the kind on show, what it looks for and where you are among its marks ("2 of 12"), with arrows to go from one to the next (also ⌃⌘G and ⇧⌃⌘G), a pop-up to switch kinds and Done to turn it off. - **Hold the pointer over a marked word** to see why it's marked ("Echo: “treat” is used again 41 words later."), or Control-click it for the same note, Next Highlight and Turn Off Highlights. With the insertion point in an echo, both its uses are tinted more strongly. - **A Revision tab in the inspector** (⌃⌘7) lists every kind with how many the scene or chapter chosen has. Click one to highlight it; it opens to say what it looks for, list what it found and hold its settings, such as how near an echo is and how long a long sentence. Click a found word or sentence to go to it, and again for the next. Under Overused Words, a badge such as "8×" means the scene uses a word eight times as often as the book does. - **Project › Revision Report…** shows the whole book's most-used words, repeated phrases and watch-list words in place of the binder, each with the places it's written. - **Project › Watch List…** keeps your own crutch words and phrases, one a line; "seem*" matches any ending. English projects start with a short list: "just", "really", "very" and others. - **Ignore “word” as an Echo**: Control-click an echo that's meant, in the text or the Revision tab, and it's no longer marked in this project. **Mark Again** brings it back. - **Settings › Writer › Language tagging** chooses whether the Mac's on-device language tagging helps find them; it's on unless you turn it off. - **With VoiceOver**, each mark is said with why it's marked, and the rotor moves between them. With Differentiate Without Color, they're underlined too. - **Help**: a new page, Revision aids, under Revising.
## Revision passes
See what you've changed in a draft, and put back what you cut.
- **Project › Start Revision Pass…** names a pass ("Draft 2"), gives it a color and, if you like, a cut goal of a number of words or a share such as 10%. Foolscap keeps a snapshot of each scene in the Manuscript as it is, "Before Draft 2". **Project › End Revision Pass** ends it. Both can be undone. - **View › Revision Highlights › Changes** tints the words you've added during the pass in its color, and puts a small mark where you cut words. Hold the pointer over the mark to see what you cut, or click it to see the words and **Put Back** to put them back as they were. - **All Passes** tints each word in the color of the pass that added it, for the last four passes. - **The Revision tab** shows the pass: its dates, the words added and cut across the Manuscript, and how far you are toward the cut goal, with Changes listing each change in the scene. - **Project › Revision Report… › Changes** lists every scene the pass changed, made or removed, with its words added and cut, and each change, a cut shown as it read before. - **The Snapshots tab** marks each pass's starting snapshot with a dot in its color, and warns before you delete one. **Show Changes in Text**, on any snapshot's shortcut menu, marks what changed since it in the text itself. - **Splitting and merging scenes during a pass** keeps their changes: each part has its share of the starting snapshot. - **With VoiceOver**, each cut mark is a button that says what was cut, with Show Cut Words and Put Back. - **Help**: Revision passes, on the Revision aids page.
## The book's shape
- **View › Book Shape** shows the whole Manuscript in place of the text: a bar for each scene in book order, grouped by chapter, its height its words. Color the bars by **Status**, **Chapter**, **Dialogue** or the **Revision Pass** (the words added, and those cut as an outline). A thinner row under them shows each scene's dialogue, or in non-fiction, its sentences' average length. Hover over a bar for the scene's title, words and synopsis; click it to choose the scene, double-click to open it. - **The Revision tab's Shape** shows how much of the scene is dialogue, how many sentences it has and how long they are on average, with a chart of its sentences' lengths in order. A line under the bars marks five or more sentences in a row much the same length; click a bar to select its sentence. - **Help**: The book's shape, and the shape of a scene, on the Revision aids page.
## VoiceOver
The start of a pass to make Foolscap work with VoiceOver and the keyboard alone.
- **VoiceOver says what each object in the text is.** A picture is read as an image with its description, or "no description" when it has none; a footnote as "footnote 1" where its marker is and "end of footnote" after its words; a page break and a scene break by name, not as three asterisks. A hidden footnote is read as only its number. - **Tables can be read and edited with VoiceOver.** A table is read as "table, 3 rows, 2 columns", and VoiceOver can go into it row by row; each cell is named by its row and, in a table with a header row, its column's heading. - **VoiceOver's rotor moves through the text** by headings, footnotes, comments, bookmarks, images and tables, listing each by its words, so you can jump to one as you'd glance down the page. - **Comments and bookmarks are said on their words**, as annotations: "Comment: Check the date", or the bookmark's name. A citation or cross-reference is read as the words it shows, with "not found" when it's red. - **Corkboard cards are read as cards**: each by its title, status, day and synopsis, with actions to open, rename and move it. - **The timeline says which card you've chosen** as you move with the arrow keys, and its Who's Where lanes read as a line per character: the days, scenes and places they're in. - **Page Preview's pages are named**, "Page 3 of 12", each with a way to see it up close and back, and the bar's pop-ups are named too. - **The status bar's messages are spoken** as they show, such as "Snapshot taken". - **A split editor's panes are named**, "Left pane" and "Right pane" (or top and bottom), so you can tell which you're in. - **Progress's chart is read a day at a time**, with each day's words and the daily goal. Before, VoiceOver read it as spans of two days. - **More is named**: a picture shown on its own, by its description; the full-page picture's bar; the Notes' synopsis; the Snapshots list; the References window's list, button and fields; and the Help buttons, by what they open. - **Open Quickly says the result you've chosen** as you press ↑ and ↓, and the first one once you stop typing: "Chapter 3, Manuscript, 1 of 12". - **Find in Project says what it found**, "65 matches in 8 scenes", once you stop typing, and how many it replaced; each item in the results says its number of matches. - **Import's outline says what each row is**, "Chapter 1, chapter, 2,400 words", rather than its icon's name. - **Goals: the words-a-day field has moved.** Under Each day, choose **A number of words** and the field shows under it. Before, it was inside its choice, where VoiceOver couldn't reach it. - **The sheets' titles are headings**, and their Help buttons, fields and lists are named. - **The picture pop-over's controls are named** by the labels beside them, and its sliders say their width or size.
## The keyboard
- **Bookmarks can be reordered from the keyboard.** Choose one and press **⌃⌘↑** or **⌃⌘↓** (Project › Move), or Control-click it for Move Up and Move Down. - **The Story Bible's picture can be chosen from the keyboard.** With keyboard navigation on, Tab to it and press Space; Delete removes it. - **Project › Move › To Front Matter, To Manuscript, To Back Matter, To Story Bible and To Notes** move what's chosen in the binder or on the corkboard to the end of that section, as dragging it there does. - **View › Inspector › Comments (⌃⌘4) and Bookmarks (⌃⌘5) put you in the list**, as Notes already did. Press ↑ and ↓ to go from one to the next, and **Esc** to go back to the text. - **The arrow keys go into a table.** Before, a cell could be reached only by clicking. Coming to a table from the text above it, or from just before it, goes into its first cell; from below, into its last row; from just after it, into its last cell. They already left the table at its edges. - **Project › Move works on the corkboard's cards.** With a card selected, ⌃⌘↑ and ⌃⌘↓ move it earlier or later, ⌃⌘→ puts it in the chapter card before it, and ⌃⌘← takes it out of the chapter. Before, they moved the chapter the board belongs to.
## Help
- **A new Accessibility page** gathers what VoiceOver says in the text and its rotors, a keyboard way for everything done by dragging, and the display settings Foolscap follows. Choose Help › Foolscap Help and look under Settings and shortcuts.
## Display settings
- **Reduce Motion** stops typewriter scrolling gliding and Focus Mode sliding the sidebar and inspector shut. - **Increase Contrast** makes the tints on comments, footnotes, citations and bookmarked passages stronger. - **Increase Contrast and Differentiate Without Color** mark the active pane of a split editor with a line, not just a tint; with Differentiate Without Color, a citation or cross-reference that isn't found has a dashed outline. - **Snapshot comparisons are easier to read**: added words are underlined on green, in the text's own color, instead of in green.

## Pictures in a line
A small picture, such as the button in "click the ⚙ button", can now sit among the words of a sentence instead of on a line of its own.
- **Insert, drag or paste a picture under 100 pixels tall among words**, and it goes in the line. Rich text pasted from another app keeps its small pictures in their lines. - **Click any picture and choose In Line or Own Line** to move it. A larger picture inserted mid-sentence goes on a line of its own; In Line puts it back among the words. A picture in a line has a **Size** in ems, from 0.5 to 2: one em is the size of the type around it, so an icon in a heading is larger than one in the text. - **Its middle lines up with the middle of the lowercase letters**, in the editor and in every export: reading copies, manuscripts, paperbacks, Word, EPUB, RTF and Markdown. In an ebook it grows and shrinks with the reader's type. - **It isn't a figure**: no caption or number, though it still has a description for readers who can't see it. - **Imports keep them.** A picture in a sentence in a Word, RTF or Scrivener document comes in where it was, if it's no taller than twice the type. Scrivener's Tutorial now keeps its toolbar icons in their sentences instead of splitting the paragraphs round them.
## Paperbacks
- **A book with no front matter starts on its first page.** A paperback whose Front Matter is empty or hidden, as a project imported from Scrivener or a document can be, opened on two blank pages. Its text now starts on page 1. - **The Export sheet says when a paperback has no title page.** KDP and IngramSpark both ask for one. Add it with the **+** button in the Front Matter. - **The paperback and the ebook have their own ISBNs.** The Copyright page in the Front Matter has a **Paperback ISBN** and an **Ebook ISBN**, as the two editions need different ones and a Kindle ebook needs none. Each edition's copyright page shows only its own. An ISBN you'd already entered is now the paperback's; if it was your ebook's, move it to **Ebook ISBN**. - **Fewer lines about low-resolution pictures.** The Export sheet gives one line for a scene's pictures, however many there are, with the lowest resolution among them, rather than a line for each.

## All the pages at a glance
**View › Page Preview** (⌥⌘P) now opens on all the pages, set out in rows, as many to a row as fit. You can see the shape of the whole book at once: where chapters open, where full-page images fall, which pages run short. A paperback's facing pages stay together in pairs. A scene of only a page or two is shown as large as the window allows, as before.
The rows fit themselves to the window again when you make it wider or narrower.
## A page up close
**Double-click a page** to look at it closely, or double-tap it with two fingers on a trackpad. The pointer over the pages is a magnifying glass to remind you.
- **The page is shown at its real size**, or larger if the pages were small, with the pages before and after it above and below. A paperback's page has its facing page beside it. - **The bar says where you are**: "Page 12 of 240", or "Pages 12–13 of 240" in a paperback. - **To go back to all the pages**, click **All Pages** in the bar, double-click again, press Esc, or choose **View › Zoom to Fit** (⌘9). Choosing another layout, or something else to preview, also goes back. With all the pages showing, Esc leaves Page Preview, as before.
**View › Zoom In**, **Zoom Out** and **Actual Size**, and pinching on a trackpad, still work in either view.
## Fonts you can see before you choose
The format bar's font menu now shows each font's name in the font itself, so you can see how it looks before you choose it. Fonts of symbols, such as Wingdings, and fonts for other alphabets are named in the system font. The menu's button still shows the chosen font's name in the system font, as the rest of the bar does.

## Lists of figures and tables
Two new pages for the Front Matter: **List of Figures** and **List of Tables**. Click **+** on the Front Matter's heading to add one. Each goes after the Contents and lists every captioned figure or table with its number, caption and page: "Figure 2.1. Map of the valley ... 34".
A figure is an image with a caption under it. A table is listed when it has a caption: type a line just under it and choose **Format › Caption** (⌥⌘7). In the editor, each list page shows what it will list. Click an entry to go to that figure or table.
The lists are offered while **View › Tools › Cross-References and Numbering** is on. A list with nothing in it is dimmed and left out.
## A Contents that goes deeper
The Contents page has a new **Lists** pop-up menu:
- **Chapters**: parts and chapters, as before. - **Chapters and Sections**: the sections in each chapter too, and headings you type one level below a chapter's title. - **Down to Subheadings**: one level further.
## Page numbers in more exports
The Contents and the lists now show page numbers wherever there are pages:
- **Paperback PDF**, as before, now with the lists. - **Reading Copy PDF**, which now includes the Contents and lists. - **A paper's PDF**, and printing. - **Word**, as Word's own table of contents and table of figures. They come filled in with Foolscap's page numbers. Choose **Update Field** in Word for Word's own numbers, which may differ a little.
In an **ebook**, the lists are pages of links, and readers' apps can find them. **Markdown** asks Pandoc to make the Contents and lists. **RTF** leaves them out, as it has no page numbers.
## Chicago Thesis
**Project › Manuscript Format…** has a new format, **Chicago Thesis (Turabian 9)**, for a thesis or dissertation:
- **A thesis title page**: your institution at the top, the title, a statement of what it's submitted for, your department, "by" and your name, and the place and month at the foot. The Title Page has new **Institution**, **Statement**, **Department** and **Place** fields. - **Front matter numbered in roman numerals** at the foot of the page (ii, iii, iv), and the text from 1, at the top right. - **Each chapter starts a new page.**
Its headings, notes and bibliography are the same as Chicago Student Paper's.
## Two new templates
- **Thesis**: the Chicago Thesis format, with a Title Page, Abstract, Contents, List of Figures, List of Tables and Acknowledgments; an Introduction, two chapters and a Conclusion; and an Appendix and Bibliography. Change the degree in its statement to yours. - **Scholarly Book**: the Non-Fiction Book, with Chicago notes and bibliography, figures and tables numbered by chapter, and lists of them after the Contents.
## A new About window
**Foolscap › About Foolscap** now shows the version and build, with buttons for the acknowledgements and the Foolscap website.
### Your projects
Foolscap 0.9.4 can still open a project saved with this version. But it leaves out the lists of figures and tables, sets a thesis out as a fiction manuscript, and shows its Contents as Chapters. If you save the project in 0.9.4, these settings are lost.

## Footnotes in a pop-over
Choose **Insert › Footnote** (⌥⌘E) and the note's number goes into the text, with a pop-over beside it for the note's words. Press Return or Escape, or click back in the text, and carry on writing. A new note you close without writing anything is taken out again.
- **To change a note**, double-click its number, or select it and choose **Insert › Edit Footnote…** (⌥⌘E). - **To remove a note**, click the trash can in its pop-over. - **The pop-over's bar** has what a note can hold: bold, italic, underline and highlight, and in a project that uses them, citations and cross-references. **Edit › Undo** takes back what you wrote in one step.
A new project now starts with its footnotes hidden, so each note shows just its number. Hold the pointer over a number to read the note, or choose **View › Show Footnotes** to see them all in the text. To show or hide one note, Option-double-click its number.
## Endnotes
You can now have your notes printed as endnotes. Choose **Project › Manuscript Format…** and pick one under **Notes**:
- **Footnotes, at the foot of each page**, as before. - **Endnotes, after each chapter**: each chapter's notes are listed under "Notes" at its end. - **Endnotes, at the end of the book** (or paper): every note is listed together on the new **Notes** page in the Back Matter. Choosing this adds the page before the works cited. Drag it to put the notes elsewhere.
You still write every note as a footnote. Your choice is for every export and printout but Markdown. Choosing MLA in Manuscript Format picks endnotes, as MLA has them, and APA picks footnotes.
## Numbering notes
Manuscript Format can also set how notes are numbered:
- **Numbered:** 1, 2, 3; i, ii, iii; a, b, c; or \*, †, ‡. - **Start again:** never, at each chapter, or, for footnotes, on each page.
The editor shows notes numbered the same way. It can't show pages, though, so with **On each page** it starts again at each chapter instead.
## Fixes
- **Cancel** now closes the citation, cross-reference and image pop-overs.
### Your projects
Earlier versions of Foolscap can still open a project saved with this version, but they ignore these settings and print its notes as footnotes, numbered 1, 2, 3.

## Front Matter and Back Matter
Everything that comes before and after your manuscript now has a place of its own in the binder: **Front Matter** above the Manuscript and **Back Matter** below it. The pages are in the order the book prints them. Drag them to change the order, and delete one to leave it out.
- **Pages Foolscap makes for you**, such as the Cover, Title Page, Copyright, Contents and References. Choose one to change what it says: the cover image, the title and subtitle, the copyright lines. These used to be in Book Details. - **Pages you write**, such as a dedication, acknowledgements or an about the author page. These are texts like any other. A Dedication is centered on its page. - **A paper's pages.** In APA, MLA and Chicago, the Front Matter holds the Title Page (MLA's Heading) and the Abstract, with its keywords above its text. The Back Matter holds the References, Works Cited or Bibliography, wherever you put it.
Click **+** on either heading to add a page. A page with nothing on it yet is dimmed and left out. To hide both sections, choose **View › Tools › Front and Back Matter**.
The Reading Copy and Other Formats exports have a new **Front and back matter** checkbox. Markdown puts the title, author and copyright in its metadata.
**Book Details** is now **Project › Paperback Settings…**, which keeps just the paperback's trim size, typeface and paper. A paper doesn't show it.
### Your projects
When you open a project made with an earlier Foolscap, it moves into the new sections. Its title page, copyright page and cover become pages, with an empty Cover to fill in if it had none. Its dedication becomes a Dedication text. The notes it used as front and back matter, and a paper's abstract, move in too. Your exports come out as they did before.
Once it's saved, Foolscap 0.9.2 and earlier can't open the project.
Show hide features based on document type

## Foolscap updates itself
Foolscap now looks for updates once a day and offers to install them, with a note like this one saying what's new. You can also choose **Foolscap › Check for Updates…** at any time.
To change how often it looks, or to have updates installed when you quit, open **Foolscap › Settings…** and choose **Updates**.
